summary: Summarizes how hashes are used in many Internet protocols and discusses how newly found collision attacks do or do not affect them. It shows how to thwart known attacks on digital certificates and outlines directions for protocol designers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Hashes are like fingerprints for data. When researchers found ways to make two things share one fingerprint, people worried. This memo checks which protocols are really at risk.

questions: do hash collisions break internet protocols
what is a hash collision attack
difference between collision and preimage attack
subtitle: Which Internet protocols are really hurt by collision attacks on MD5 and SHA-1, and what to do about it.

tldr.problem: Newly announced collision attacks on MD5 and SHA-1 led to confused debate about whether common Internet protocols were broken.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the properties of hash algorithms, surveys how protocols use them, and shows that only digital signatures (messages and certificates) are meaningfully affected by collision attacks.
tldr.outcome: It advises moving away from MD5 and SHA-1, especially MD5, and making protocols able to switch hash algorithms, although its two authors disagree on how fast.

today: RFC 4270 is an Informational document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records what was known and advised as of November 2005.

sections.title: Hash Algorithms and the Attacks on Them
sections.content:
A "perfect" hash algorithm turns data of any size into a fixed-size hash value, of length L. Two properties follow. Finding two messages with the same hash takes about 2^(L/2) attempts (collision free), and finding another message matching a given message's hash takes 2^L attempts (one way).

An imperfect algorithm lets an attacker do less work. A collision attack finds two messages with the same hash in fewer than 2^(L/2) attempts. A first-preimage attack finds a message for a known hash in fewer than 2^L attempts, and a second-preimage attack finds a second message matching a given one in fewer than 2^L attempts.

All the practical or almost-practical attacks known at the time on MD5 and SHA-1 were collision attacks, which the RFC calls fortunate, since preimage attacks would be much more devastating. The collision attacks also need at least one of the two messages to have a fair amount of structure.
sections.plainLanguage: A fingerprint should be unique to each person. A collision attack is finding two people with the same fingerprint; a preimage attack is forging a fingerprint for a particular person, which is much harder.

sections.title: The Situation in 2005
sections.content:
In summer 2004 a team showed MD5 was susceptible to collision attacks. In early 2005 the same team showed a similar attack on a variant of SHA-1 and predicted the normal SHA-1 would also fall to a large amount of work. Researchers also showed a construction for PKIX certificates that use MD5 for signing, and another showed a faster way to find MD5 collisions (eight hours on a 1.6-GHz computer).

The summary given: attacks on both exist, with MD5 much worse; MD5 attacks are practical on any modern computer; SHA-1 attacks are not feasible with today's computers but may be if they improve or computing gets cheaper; many protocols use hashes in ways these attacks do not affect; and most affected protocols use digital signatures. The conservative approach is an orderly migration away from SHA-1 and MD5, especially MD5.
sections.plainLanguage: People found cracks in two popular fingerprint methods. One crack is big and easy to use; the other is small for now but may widen.

sections.title: How Protocols Use Hashes
sections.content:
The RFC lists the uses of hashes: non-repudiable signatures on messages (S/MIME and OpenPGP), signatures in certificates from trusted third parties, challenge-response protocols, message authentication with shared secrets, key derivation functions, mixing functions, and integrity checks of files against a hash received out of band.

Only the first two, the digital-signature uses, are affected by collision attacks, and then only in limited circumstances. Challenge-response is believed safe because the sender authenticates a secret the recipient already has. Shared-secret authentication is believed safe because both parties know the secret. Key derivation functions in IETF protocols take random input from both parties, so an attacker cannot structure the hashed message.
sections.plainLanguage: Most fingerprint uses are safe because the cheater cannot choose what gets fingerprinted. The risky ones are when a person signs a paper someone else prepared.

sections.title: Signatures and Certificates
sections.content:
In a signature attack, the attacker creates two messages with the same hash, gets one signed, and presents the signature with the other. The canonical example is a message promising to pay $10 versus one promising $10,000. To thwart it where a human judges the signed message, the signer should keep a copy of the original message he or she signed; two different messages with the same hash do not arise by accident, so the doubt should defeat the attack. Automated settings such as EDI are harder, and need a detailed evaluation.

For certificates, the 2005 attack on PKIX needed the attacker to predict the contents before issuance, including identity, serial number and validity dates. The net effect is one identity getting a certificate over one public key but pretending it is over a different key with the same identity, so there is probably no real-world advantage. Collision attacks only touch parts without human-readable information, such as public keys.

A certificate authority can reduce the risk by making other signed parts less predictable: part of the serial number unpredictable, a random component added to the identity, or validity dates skewed forwards or backwards.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone tricks you into signing a note and swaps it later, keeping your own copy proves what you really signed. An issuer can also add a surprise detail so the cheater cannot prepare in advance.

sections.title: Where to Go from Here
sections.content:
The authors disagree on what to do now. One argues for migrating to SHA-256 (256-bit hash length) immediately, since attacks only get better and it is better to move before a panic. The other argues the collision attacks have shown no discernible real-world effect, it is unclear which stronger algorithm is best long term, and switching causes interoperability problems; he would change his view if practical attacks appeared.

They agree that all Internet protocols should be able to use different hash algorithms with longer hash values, and any new protocol must be able to change all of its cryptographic algorithms, not just its hash. The security considerations note that significant preimage attacks had already been discovered but were not yet practical, and a practical one would drastically affect many protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: One author says to switch to a stronger fingerprint now; the other says to wait for a reason. Both say every system should be built so the fingerprint method can be swapped.
